name: The danger zone (40–140°F)
scope: The core mechanism the whole sub-strand hangs on: bacteria breed fastest in a warm window. T1: perishable food left out at room temperature turns unsafe because that warmth (roughly 40–140°F) is exactly the range where food bacteria multiply fastest — the 'danger zone' (number in the stem, the concept is the answer). T2: HOW fast — in that zone bacteria can DOUBLE about every 20 minutes, which is why the rule is 2 hours out at most (1 hour on a hot day above 90°F). T3: the two-sided rule — you dodge the zone by keeping hot food hot (above 140°F on a steam table) and cold food cold (below 40°F over ice); a buffet is a race against the middle. T4: cooling a big pot of chili on the counter is the sneaky trap — the CORE sits in the danger zone for hours while the top cools; splitting it into shallow containers drops the center below 40°F fast. T5: 'just reheat it' is not a reset — reheating to 165°F kills living bacteria, but some (like Staph) already left behind a heat-proof TOXIN that boiling won't undo, so long time in the zone can't always be cooked away.
source: USDA FSIS 'Danger Zone (40°F–140°F)' and 'How Temperatures Affect Food'; USDA FSIS 'Leftovers and Food Safety'. (Grokipedia attempted first per source priority but returned HTTP 403 and the Chrome bridge was offline; corroborated on the primary agency.)
framing_note: Scene-led; invert the wonder — put the scary number/superlative in the stem (doubling every 20 min) and make the KNOWABLE concept the answer. The canonical round safety figures (40–140°F, 20 min, 2-hour rule) ARE the practical payload a father wants retrievable, so a rung may answer with the round figure, but steer most rungs to the WHY. Keep the 'fridge SLOWS but doesn't kill' fact OUT of here (it lives in the fridge/freezer ladder) to avoid a same-fact repeat. Prep-frame voice fine. Dinner-test payoff = T5 (reheating can't undo a pre-formed toxin).

name: Safe internal temperatures — and why they differ
scope: One number per food, each for a concrete reason. T1: a steak can be safely eaten pink in the middle but a burger can't — because on a whole cut the bacteria live only on the SURFACE, and searing the outside kills them while the interior stays nearly sterile. T2: grinding changes everything — it mixes that surface bacteria all through the batch, so ground beef has no safe pink middle and must reach 160°F throughout. T3: chicken and all poultry go to 165°F, no exceptions — salmonella and campylobacter can ride throughout the bird, so poultry is the one you always cook fully. T4: whole cuts of beef and pork are done at 145°F WITH a 3-minute rest — off the heat the interior keeps climbing (carryover) and the juices settle back in. T5 (food-history payoff): pork used to be cooked gray at 160°F+ because of the trichinella worm (trichinosis); modern indoor hog farming almost erased it, so in 2011 the USDA lowered safe pork to 145°F and a rosy pork chop became fine. T5: color is a liar — a burger can brown before it's safe or stay pink after it is; only a thermometer in the center tells the truth (doneness vs safety).
source: USDA FSIS 'Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart'; FSIS 'Doneness Versus Safety' and 'Color of Cooked Ground Beef'; USDA 2011 pork guidance 160→145°F + 3-min rest (USDA blog / CIDRAP); FSIS 'Ground Beef and Food Safety'.
framing_note: Scene-led (the pink-burger-vs-pink-steak puzzle), never 'what temp is safe for X?' as a definition-shell. The canonical temps (165/160/145) are precisely the retrievable safety facts a parent wants, so answering with the round temp is allowed here — but pair each with its WHY so it reads as reasoning, not rote. ACCURACY RAIL: pork is 145°F since 2011 (never say it 'must be 160'); attribute the parasite correctly (trichinella → pork). Keep the 'grinding spreads surface bacteria' mechanism HERE and don't restate it in the E. coli ladder. Dinner-test payoff = T5 (the pork-temperature history).

name: Cross-contamination — how outbreaks actually start
scope: The invisible hand-off from raw to ready-to-eat. T1: the classic kitchen mistake — cutting raw chicken and then chopping salad on the same unwashed board and knife; the raw-meat juices carry bacteria onto food that gets no cooking step to kill them. T2: the fix pros use — separate boards, often color-coded (red for raw meat, green for produce), or wash-and-sanitize between jobs. T3: the fridge drip — raw meat parked ABOVE ready-to-eat food drips onto it, so raw meat belongs on the BOTTOM shelf in a sealed dish. T4 (amazing-fact payoff): the dirtiest thing in the whole kitchen is usually the SPONGE — damp, warm, and full of food bits, it's a bacterial hotel; microwaving it wet or swapping it out beats wiping germs around. T5: the BBQ classic — carrying cooked burgers back on the same plate that held the raw patties, or brushing on leftover raw-meat marinade as a sauce (boil it first, or set some aside before it touches the meat).
source: USDA FSIS 'Washing Raw Poultry: Our Science, Your Choice' (2019 study: 26% transferred bacteria to salad lettuce); FSIS cutting-board / cross-contamination guidance; FDA 'Four Steps to Food Safety' (Clean / Separate).
framing_note: Scene-led — each rung is a concrete kitchen moment, never 'define cross-contamination'. The answer is always the food/technique (separate boards, bottom shelf, the sponge, boil the marinade), never a bare rule or agency. Prep-frame voice fine. Dinner-test payoff = T4 (the sponge is the dirtiest thing in the house). Keep the 'don't RINSE chicken' fact out of here — it's its own ladder.

name: Salmonella — the egg-and-poultry germ
scope: The pathogen behind raw-egg risk, told through the foods that carry it. T1: licking the cake-batter spoon or eating homemade Caesar dressing/eggnog carries a salmonella risk — from the raw EGGS in them (egg is the answer). T2: it isn't only on the shell — a hen can pass salmonella INTO the egg before the shell even forms, so a clean, uncracked egg can still carry it raw. T3: that's why pasteurized eggs exist — gently heated in the shell to kill salmonella without cooking, so a kitchen can serve raw-egg Caesar or eggnog safely. T4: the kill step at home is heat — cook until the white AND yolk are firm; a runny sunny-side-up yolk is the higher-risk one. T5 (surprising payoff): raw SPROUTS (alfalfa, mung) are a top salmonella carrier too — the warm, humid days it takes seeds to sprout are also perfect for bacteria to bloom, and you eat sprouts raw.
source: CDC 'Salmonella and Eggs'; FDA 'Egg Safety' and pasteurized-egg guidance; CDC raw-cookie-dough and sprouts outbreak pages; Cleveland Clinic / WebMD raw-dough explainers.
framing_note: Scene-led (the batter spoon), invert the wonder. The tested answer is always a FOOD or the kill technique (eggs, pasteurized eggs, firm yolk, raw sprouts) — 'salmonella' is the hook/context, never make a Latin binomial the answer. ACCURACY RAIL: don't imply washing the shell makes a raw egg safe (it can be inside the egg). Dinner-test payoff = T5 (raw sprouts). Keep the raw-FLOUR risk out of here — it belongs in the E. coli ladder.

name: E. coli — burgers, greens, and the outbreak that changed the rules
scope: A toxin-making germ and its two surprising vehicles, plus the case that rewrote US rules. T1: the food most tied to dangerous E. coli (the O157 strain) is the undercooked hamburger — it makes a toxin that hits kids especially hard, which is why a burger's middle must be fully cooked. T2 (counterintuitive payoff): leafy greens — romaine, spinach, sprouts — are the OTHER big E. coli source; cattle runoff or dirty irrigation water lands on leaves you eat RAW, so a bagged salad can carry more risk than a well-cooked burger. T3: raw FLOUR carries it too — grain picks up E. coli out in the field and flour is never treated to kill it, so raw cookie dough is risky even with no egg in it. T4 (food-history payoff): the 1993 Jack in the Box outbreak — undercooked fast-food burgers sickened hundreds and killed four children; it pushed burger cook-temps up and made E. coli O157 an illegal 'adulterant' in US ground beef.
source: CDC E. coli and leafy greens; CDC 'Raw Flour and Dough'; Wikipedia '1992–1993 Jack in the Box E. coli outbreak'; FDA raw-dough guidance; USDA FSIS 'Ground Beef and Food Safety'.
framing_note: Scene-led. The tested answer is the FOOD/vehicle (the pink burger, raw greens, raw flour) or the food-history beat — the strain code 'O157:H7' stays context/distractor, never the tested answer. Handle the four child deaths matter-of-factly, not gorily (kid audience). ACCURACY RAIL: it's GROUND beef, not steak; do NOT restate the 'grinding spreads surface bacteria' mechanism here (that's the temps ladder) — here the payoff is that GREENS and FLOUR are the sneaky vehicles. Dinner-test payoff = T2 (a salad can out-risk a cooked burger).

name: Listeria — the germ that grows in your fridge
scope: The exception to 'the cold keeps it safe.' T1: nearly all food bacteria stall in the cold — but one dangerous germ, listeria, keeps slowly GROWING even at fridge temperature, so the fridge isn't a safe hiding spot from it. T2: its home foods are the ready-to-eat cold ones — deli meats and hot dogs, and soft cheeses like brie, feta, and queso fresco, especially those made from unpasteurized milk. T3: that's why pregnant women are told to skip cold deli meat and soft cheese (or heat deli meat until steaming) — listeria can cross the placenta and harm the baby even when the mother barely feels ill. T4 (food payoff): it's the whole reason raw-milk cheese is regulated — pasteurizing the milk is the kill step, so the raw-milk-cheese debate trades a fuller flavor against exactly this risk.
source: FDA 'Listeria (Food Safety for Moms-to-Be)'; CDC Listeria (deli meats and soft cheeses); Mayo Clinic 'Listeria infection'; FDA raw-milk-cheese guidance.
framing_note: Scene-led (the fridge that isn't safe). The tested answer is the FOOD or mechanism (soft cheese, deli meat, the pasteurization kill step) — 'Listeria monocytogenes' Latin name is context only. Handle the pregnancy risk factually and calmly, not alarmist. Dinner-test payoff = T1 (a germ that grows in the cold). vision NOT mandated — the raw-milk point is framed as a settled flavor-vs-risk trade, a factual rung, not a stance.

name: Wash your hands — 20 seconds and the soap trick
scope: Why the boring rule actually works. T1: the moment that matters most while cooking is right AFTER handling raw chicken, meat, or eggs and BEFORE you touch anything ready-to-eat — that's when hands ferry germs onto food. T2 (mechanism): soap doesn't mostly KILL germs — it LIFTS them; one end of a soap molecule grabs grease and germs while the other grabs water, so a rinse carries them away. T3: that's why it takes about 20 seconds — the soap needs time to surround the grease into tiny bubbles and your scrubbing friction to pry germs loose; a 2-second splash barely dents them. T4 (payoff): hand sanitizer is a backup, not a substitute — it kills many germs but doesn't wash away grease or dirt and works poorly on norovirus, so soap-and-water wins whenever hands are greasy or visibly dirty.
source: CDC 'Handwashing Facts' / Clean Hands; Northeastern Global News surfactant/micelle explainer ('why 20 seconds'); FDA 'Four Steps to Food Safety' (Clean).
framing_note: Scene-led, mechanism-forward — the payoff is that soap LIFTS rather than kills (T2). The answer is the technique/mechanism, never 'the CDC recommends'. Prep-frame voice fine. The 20-second figure is canonical practical payload, fine as an answer once, but the richer rung answers WHY 20s. Dinner-test payoff = T4 (sanitizer is only a backup and is weak on norovirus).

name: Don't rinse raw chicken
scope: A gem that reverses a common habit. T1: contrary to what many home cooks do, you should NOT rinse raw chicken under the tap before cooking. T2 (mechanism): the splashing spray aerosolizes the chicken's bacteria (salmonella, campylobacter) up to a few feet around the sink — onto counters, dish towels, and any salad sitting nearby. T3 (payoff): rinsing doesn't even remove those bacteria — they cling to the meat, and only cooking to 165°F kills them — so the rinse is pure risk with zero benefit; pat it dry with a paper towel instead if you want a better sear.
source: USDA FSIS 'Washing Raw Poultry: Our Science, Your Choice' (2019 study); Cleveland Clinic 'Should You Wash Raw Chicken?'; Ohio State CFAES 'Chow Line'.
framing_note: Scene-led — the surprise (the rule reverses a common habit) is the hook. The answer is the technique/mechanism (don't rinse; it splashes; cooking is the only kill). ACCURACY RAIL: patting dry improves searing — keep that a bonus, not the safety claim. Dinner-test payoff = T3 (all risk, no benefit). Distinct from the cross-contamination ladder — this one is specifically the rinse myth.

name: Safe thawing — never on the counter
scope: Getting a frozen bird to the pan without a bacterial party. T1: the three safe ways to thaw are in the FRIDGE (safest, slow), in COLD water in a sealed bag (change the water every 30 minutes), or in the MICROWAVE — the fridge is the no-planning-required default. T2 (mechanism payoff): why NOT the counter — the OUTSIDE of the food thaws and sits warming in the danger zone, growing bacteria for hours, while the CENTER is still a block of ice. T3: microwave-thawed food must be cooked IMMEDIATELY, because the microwave warms the edges into the danger zone and even starts cooking spots. T4: food thawed safely in the FRIDGE can be refrozen (with some quality loss), but counter-thawed food cannot — that's safety, not fussiness.
source: USDA FSIS 'The Big Thaw — Safe Defrosting Methods'; FSIS 'Freezing and Food Safety'; USDA ask.usda.gov thawing FAQs.
framing_note: Scene-led (thawing a chicken for dinner). The answer is the technique/mechanism (the fridge; the surface-vs-core reason; cook-immediately). Prep-frame voice fine. Dinner-test payoff = T2 (the surface thaws into the danger zone while the core is still frozen). Don't re-teach the 40–140 numbers as the answer here — reference them, but this ladder's payoff is the surface/core insight.

name: Clean vs sanitize — two different jobs
scope: Why a shiny counter can still be dangerous. T1: cleaning and sanitizing aren't the same step — cleaning REMOVES the visible dirt, grease, and food bits; sanitizing REDUCES the invisible germs; a counter can look spotless and still be germy. T2 (mechanism payoff): you must CLEAN first, THEN sanitize — because leftover grease and food scraps physically shield germs, so a sanitizer sprayed on a dirty surface can't even reach them. T3: the sanitizing tools are heat (a dishwasher's hot final rinse) or a chemical (a diluted bleach or sanitizer solution), and it has to stay WET on the surface for its 'contact time' to work. T4: let a sanitized surface AIR-dry — wiping it with a used towel just smears the germs back on.
source: Cornell Produce Safety Alliance 'Cleaning vs. Sanitizing'; StateFoodSafety 'Cleaning and Sanitizing'; FDA / ServSafe clean-then-sanitize guidance.
framing_note: Scene-led (the shiny-but-germy counter). The answer is the concept/technique (clean removes vs sanitize reduces; clean-before-sanitize; contact time; air-dry) — never a regulation. Prep-frame voice fine. Dinner-test payoff = T2 (grease shields germs, so a dirty surface can't actually be sanitized).

name: Best-by vs use-by vs sell-by
scope: The dates mean less about safety than people think. T1: most dates stamped on food are about QUALITY (peak flavor and freshness), not safety — a 'best if used by' yogurt is usually fine a little past it. T2: 'sell-by' is a note to the STORE for stock rotation, not a deadline for you — the food is typically good for days after. T3 (surprising payoff): the ONE date that is a true safety date — and the only one US federal law actually requires — sits on infant formula. T4 (payoff): your nose can't catch the dangerous germs — spoilage bacteria smell sour, but pathogens like salmonella and listeria don't change taste, smell, or look, so 'it seems fine' is not a safety test; go by safe-storage times instead.
source: USDA FSIS 'Food Product Dating'; Penn State Extension 'Best if Used-By vs Use-By'; FDA date-labeling guidance.
framing_note: Scene-led, invert the wonder (the surprise that the dates aren't safety dates). The answer is a food or concept (quality-not-safety; infant formula; pathogens don't smell) — never a bare law or agency as the answer, even though law is the CONTEXT of the infant-formula fact. Keep the '~30% of food wasted' figure as CONTEXT/distractor only, not a tested answer (production stat). Dinner-test payoff = T4 (dangerous pathogens don't change smell or taste).

name: Canning and botulism — the food that can hide a deadly germ
scope: A food-history flagship that ends in a real hazard. T1 (history hook): canning was invented to feed an ARMY — Napoleon's France offered a cash prize for a way to preserve food for its troops, and a cook won it by sealing food in glass jars and boiling them (the sealed, boiled jar is the answer, not the man's name). T2: it worked before anyone knew WHY — the winner had no idea about germs; decades later Pasteur showed the heat was killing the microbes that spoil food, so the boil is the real kill step. T3: the modern danger in a bad jar is botulism — from a germ that actually THRIVES with no oxygen (sealed inside a can) and makes one of the deadliest toxins known. T4: acid is the defense — high-acid foods (pickles, tomatoes, jam) are safe in a boiling-water bath, but low-acid foods (green beans, corn, meat) need a PRESSURE canner hot enough (240°F) to kill the tough spores. T5 (payoff): you can't see, smell, or taste the toxin — but a BULGING lid is the visible tell that the germ has been making gas inside, so when in doubt, throw it out. T6 (amazing fact): honey can carry botulism spores that adults shrug off but that endanger babies under one, whose guts can't fight them — which is why honey is a no for infants.
source: Wikipedia 'Nicolas Appert' (1810 prize, glass jars) and Smithsonian 'The Father of Canning'; USDA FSIS 'Clostridium botulinum & Botulism'; Univ. of Maryland / Penn State Extension home-canning botulism guidance; CDC infant botulism / honey.
framing_note: Scene-led food-history first, hazard second. ACCURACY RAILS: attribute canning to Appert's sealed GLASS JARS won via Napoleon's prize (paid 1810) — tin cans (Durand) came later; Pasteur's germ proof came DECADES after Appert, so never say Appert used germ theory. The tested answer must be the FOOD/technique/history beat (the sealed boiled jar, the pressure canner, the bulging lid, honey-and-infants), NEVER the man's name alone or the Latin 'Clostridium botulinum' (those are context/distractors). Dinner-test payoff = T5 (the bulging can) or T6 (honey and babies).

name: Cold is a brake, not a kill — fridge and freezer
scope: What refrigeration and freezing really do to germs. T1: the fridge only SLOWS bacteria; it doesn't kill them — which is exactly why leftovers still spoil if you keep them long enough. T2 (payoff): the freezer STOPS growth completely but STILL doesn't kill — bacteria go dormant and wake up when the food thaws, so a thawed food is only as safe as it was the day it went in. T3: freezer burn — those grayish, dry, leathery patches — is a QUALITY problem (moisture escaped the food), not a safety one; trim it and the rest is fine. T4: the fridge DOOR is the warmest, most temperature-swingy spot, so milk and eggs keep best on an inside shelf, not in the door bins.
source: USDA FSIS 'Freezing and Food Safety'; FSIS 'How Temperatures Affect Food'; FDA refrigerator-storage guidance.
framing_note: Scene-led (why leftovers still go bad in the cold). The answer is the mechanism/concept (slows-not-kills; dormant-and-revives; freezer burn = quality; the warm door). Dinner-test payoff = T2 (freezing doesn't kill — germs revive on thaw). This ladder OWNS the 'fridge slows but doesn't kill' fact — keep it out of the danger-zone ladder to avoid a same-fact repeat.

name: Norovirus and the sick-cook rule
scope: The most common food poisoning isn't what people expect. T1 (surprise): the number-one cause of food poisoning in the US isn't a bacterium at all — it's a virus, norovirus (the 'stomach bug'). T2: it gets into food mainly through a SICK cook handling ready-to-eat food with unwashed hands — which is why food workers must stay home when ill and why bare hands are kept off ready-to-eat food. T3 (payoff): raw OYSTERS are a classic carrier — as filter feeders they pump huge volumes of seawater and concentrate any virus from polluted water in their gut, so a raw oyster from bad water is a gamble that cooking would erase.
source: CDC 'About Norovirus'; CDC norovirus outbreaks; CDC / PMC norovirus-and-raw-oysters risk assessment.
framing_note: Scene-led, invert the wonder (the #1 cause is a virus, not bacteria — the surprise IS the answer). The tested answer is the concept/food (a virus; the sick handler; the raw oyster) — the name 'norovirus' is the hook, not a Latin puzzle. ACCURACY RAIL: cooking DOES kill it, so frame oysters as a raw-only risk, not 'unkillable'. Dinner-test payoff = T3 (oysters filter-feed and concentrate it).
